samples.text:
Choosing a career is one of the most important decision in a person's life. Some people think parents should guide their children to a particular job, but others believe young people should be free to choose. This essay will discuss both opinions.

There are some reasons why parents should guide their children. Parents have more experience of life and they know which jobs have good salary and security. Young people often do not know much about the job market and they may choose a job only because it looks exciting on TV. For example, a teenager may want to become a famous singer, but this is very difficult and most people cannot success. Also, parents usually pay for their children education, so they want them to choose a useful subject.

On the other hand, many people think young people should decide by themselves. Everyone has different interests and talents, and a job which is good for the father may not be suitable for the son. If a person is forced to study medicine or law when they are not interested, they will be unhappy and maybe they will not do the job well. In addition, the world is changing very fast, and many new jobs did not exist when the parents were young.

In my opinion, young people should choose their own career, but parents can give advice. Parents can share their experience and help their children to understand different options, but the final decision should belong to the child because they are the one who will do this job every day.

In conclusion, parents' guidance can be helpful, but I believe that young people should have freedom to choose the career they like.

samples.text:
Deciding on a career is a major step for any young person, and families often disagree about how much influence parents should have. While some argue that parents should steer their children towards a specific profession, others believe young people must be free to follow their own path. In my view, parents should offer guidance, but the final choice should rest with their children.

There are understandable reasons why parents want to direct their children's careers. Having experienced the world of work themselves, they often have a realistic understanding of which professions offer financial stability and long-term prospects. Teenagers, by contrast, may base their decisions on limited information or on idealised images of certain jobs. Parents who have invested heavily in their children's education may also feel they have a right to ensure that this investment leads to a secure future.

However, pushing a young person into a career they have not chosen can have serious consequences. People tend to perform best in work that matches their interests and abilities, and someone who studies engineering to please their parents may lack the motivation needed to succeed. They may even abandon the career later, having wasted years of training. Furthermore, the job market is changing rapidly, and the professions that parents regard as safe may not offer the same security in the future, while new fields are emerging that parents might know little about.

I believe the most constructive role for parents is that of an adviser rather than decision-maker. They can help their children explore options, arrange work experience and discuss the realities of different jobs, while respecting that it is the young person who will live with the consequences.

In conclusion, although parental guidance can prevent unrealistic choices, I believe young people should ultimately be free to choose their own careers, since genuine interest is the strongest basis for long-term success and satisfaction.

samples.text:
The extent to which parents should influence their children's choice of career is a question on which cultures and families differ considerably. Some believe that parents, with their greater experience, should direct their children towards a particular profession, while others hold that young people must be free to make this decision for themselves. My own view is that parental guidance is valuable, but only when it informs rather than overrides a young person's choice.

The argument for parental direction is not without merit. Parents generally have a clearer picture than teenagers of the practical realities of working life, including the stability, income and progression that different fields offer. Young people, meanwhile, may be drawn to glamorous but precarious occupations, or may simply lack the information to make a well-founded decision. Parents who have made sacrifices to fund their children's education can therefore feel both entitled and obliged to ensure that it leads somewhere secure.

Nevertheless, the costs of directing a child into an unwanted career can be considerable. Motivation is a powerful determinant of success, and a person who has chosen their field is far more likely to persevere through the demanding early years of a career than one who is fulfilling someone else's ambitions. Moreover, parents' knowledge of the job market is often rooted in the past; occupations that once seemed secure may be vulnerable to automation, while entirely new fields are opening up. A choice imposed on the basis of outdated assumptions may prove neither fulfilling nor safe.

Weighing these considerations, I believe parents should act as well-informed advisers. By encouraging their children to explore different options, seek work experience and think realistically about their strengths, they can help them make a sound decision without taking it out of their hands.

In conclusion, while parental experience can be a valuable resource, young people should ultimately be free to choose their own careers, since a career that is genuinely chosen is more likely to be both successful and satisfying.
